Data. Data file: data/hourly_load_factor.csv (2000 rows). The CSV we share is a derived, pre-cleaned version. For each (day, hour) of the year we have computed the hourly mean of the city-wide active power \(\overline{P}(d, h) = \mathrm{Zone1}(d, h) + \mathrm{Zone2}(d, h) + \mathrm{Zone3}(d, h)\) from the original 10-min readings, and then the hourly load factor \[\mathrm{LF}(d, h) = \frac{\overline{P}(d, h)}{\max_{h'} \overline{P}(d, h')}\,,\] i.e. the ratio between the average load in hour \(h\) and the highest hourly average of the same day. By construction \(\mathrm{LF}(d, h) \in [0, 1]\): the day-peak hour gets exactly \(1\) and the deepest off-peak hour gets the smallest value. From the full \(365 \times 24 \approx 8700\) (day, hour) cells we have taken a uniform random subsample of 2000 rows and clamped the values to \((10^{-3},\, 1 - 10^{-3})\) so that the Beta log-density is finite at the boundary.

Variables:

date : calendar date (M/D/YYYY).

hour : hour of the day, integer in \(\{0, \dots, 23\}\).

load_factor : hourly load factor as defined above, in \((10^{-3},\, 1 - 10^{-3})\).

Task.

  1. Compare a single Beta vs Beta mixture model with \(H = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\), with model selection via WAIC.

  2. Overlay the posterior predictive density on the empirical histogram and verify that the modes are recovered.

  3. Post-hoc exploration. Assign each observation to its maximum-a-posteriori component, then plot the empirical fraction of observations in each component as a function of hour.

  4. Advanced. Fit a second model which does classification on hour using the component assignment as response variable, and plot the predicted probability of each component as a function of hour. Do the two plots match? Discuss the results. (Details for this step are presented in the additional details notebook) We will predict the component assignment using a multinomial logistic regression with the Fourier-transformed hour as covariate, i.e. with predictors \(\sin(k 2\pi h / 24)\) and \(\cos(k 2\pi h / 24)\) to capture the periodicity of the day.

Task 1

Objective: Compare a single Beta vs Beta mixture model with \(H = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\), with model selection via WAIC

Mathematical Formulation: Beta Mixture Model (BMM)

A Beta Mixture Model with \(H\) components expresses the probability density function (PDF) of a continuous random variable \(X\) (where \(X \in (0,1)\)) as a convex combination of \(H\) distinct Beta distributions.

The overall density function is defined as:

\[f(x; \boldsymbol{\pi}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h \cdot \text{Beta}(x; \alpha_h, \beta_h)\]

Constraints and Parameters

  • Mixture Weights (\(\pi_h\)): Represent the probability of a data point belonging to component \(h\). They must satisfy the following conditions: \[\sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \pi_h \ge 0 \quad \forall h \in \{1, \dots, H\}\]
  • Shape Parameters (\(\alpha_h, \beta_h\)): Govern the geometry of each individual Beta density within the mixture. They must be strictly positive: \[\alpha_h > 0, \quad \beta_h > 0 \quad \forall h \in \{1, \dots, H\}\]

Component Density Function

Each individual component \(h\) is a standard Beta distribution with the following PDF:

\[\text{Beta}(x; \alpha_h, \beta_h) = \frac{1}{\text{B}(\alpha_h, \beta_h)} x^{\alpha_h - 1} (1 - x)^{\beta_h - 1}\]

where \({\text{B}(\alpha_h, \beta_h)}\) is a normalizing constant.

Model Selection via WAIC (Widely Applicable Information Criterion)

To determine the optimal number of components \(H \in \{1, \dots, 5\}\), we use WAIC, a fully Bayesian criterion that estimates the out-of-sample predictive accuracy. It is particularly suited for mixture models because it accounts for the entire posterior distribution rather than a single point estimate.

WAIC is defined as:

\[\text{WAIC} = -2 \cdot (\text{lppd} - p_{\text{WAIC}})\]

Where:

  • \(\text{lppd}\) is the log pointwise predictive density, which measures how well the model fits the observed data.
  • \(p_{\text{WAIC}}\) is the effective number of parameters, acting as a penalty for model complexity to prevent overfitting.

JAGS Model

Bayesian model and Data Augmentation

In practice, we do not know which component generated which data point. To solve this in a Bayesian framework using JAGS, we introduce a latent discrete variable \(z_i\) for each observation \(x_i\).

The variable \(z_i \in \{1, \dots, H\}\) acts as a classification label or “indicator”, telling us which sub-population the \(i\)-th data point belongs to.

Hierarchical Model Structure

We define the model hierarchically as follows:

  1. Latent Assignment (\(z_i\)): \[z_i \sim \text{Categorical}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\] This means each data point is randomly assigned to a component based on the probabilities defined by the mixture weights \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = [\pi_1, \dots, \pi_H]\).

  2. Conditional Likelihood (\(x_i \mid z_i\)): \[x_i \mid z_i \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_{z_i}, \beta_{z_i})\] Once the component \(z_i\) is assigned, the actual data point \(x_i\) is sampled from that specific Beta distribution.

Prior Distributions

To complete the Bayesian setup, we must specify prior distributions for all unknown parameters:

  • For the weights (\(\boldsymbol{\pi}\)): We use a symmetric Dirichlet distribution, which is the natural conjugate prior for categorical probabilities that must sum to 1: \[\boldsymbol{\pi} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\mathbf{1}_H)\] Where \(\mathbf{1}_H = [1, 1, \dots, 1]\) of length \(H\). This represents a flat, uninformative uniform prior over the probability simplex.

  • For the shape parameters (\(\alpha_h, \beta_h\)): Since these parameters must be strictly positive, we assign an Exponential distribution with a small rate parameter \(\lambda\): \[\alpha_h \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda), \quad \beta_h \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda) \quad \forall h \in \{1, \dots, H\}\] Setting \(\lambda = 0.1\) ensures the prior is highly diffuse (weak), allowing the data to fully drive the posterior estimation. (Later will be verified through sensitivity analysis)

Code

We import the data. For the final run we use all 2000 observations; for quick tests, set use_subsample <- TRUE to keep the runtime short. We fix the seed for reproducibility and keep hour aligned with my_data because it will be used for clustering.

set.seed(123)

# MCMC configuration 
N_CHAINS  <- 4
N_BURNIN  <- 1000
N_SAMPLES <- 2000

# Shared colour palette for the (up to five) mixture components
COMPONENT_COLS <- c("black", "darkgreen", "purple", "darkorange", "brown")

# Setup independent RNG seeds for parallel MCMC chains
make_inits <- function(n_chains = N_CHAINS, seed0 = 123) {
  lapply(seq_len(n_chains), function(c)
    list(.RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister", .RNG.seed = seed0 + c))
}

# Fourier (sine/cosine) design matrices of period 24 for a vector of hours
fourier_design <- function(h_vec, K) {
  n <- length(h_vec)
  list(S = matrix(sapply(1:K, function(k) sin(2 * pi * k * h_vec / 24)), nrow = n),
       C = matrix(sapply(1:K, function(k) cos(2 * pi * k * h_vec / 24)), nrow = n))
}

use_subsample <- FALSE
n_sub <- 400

# Subsampling for computational efficiency
if (use_subsample) {
  idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(lf)), n_sub)
} else {
  idx <- seq_len(nrow(lf))
}
lf_fit <- lf[idx, ]

my_data <- lf_fit$load_factor
N <- length(my_data)

We then define the JAGS models. Because JAGS is sensitive to model dimensioning, we use one specification for \(H = 1\) and a parametric version for the remaining cases.

The following code specifies the likelihood and priors so that JAGS can run MCMC simulations and estimate the posterior distribution.

  • The likelihood is a Beta mixture model.
    We introduce a latent categorical indicator \(Z_i\) to assign each observation \(X_i\) to one of the \(H\) components.

  • We assign weakly informative priors to all unknown parameters. In particular, we place a symmetric Dirichlet prior on the mixture weights \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) so that they sum to 1.

  • For the shape parameters \(\alpha_h\) and \(\beta_h\), we use Exponential priors with a small rate parameter (\(\lambda = 0.1\)). This keeps the parameters strictly positive while leaving the prior diffuse and weakly informative.

# Model with H=1
jags_model_H1 <- "
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    x[i] ~ dbeta(alpha, beta)
    log_lik[i] <- logdensity.beta(x[i], alpha, beta)
  }
  alpha ~ dexp(0.1)
  beta  ~ dexp(0.1)
}"

# Model for H > 1 (Beta Mixture Model with Latent Variable Z)
jags_model_mix <- "
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    z[i] ~ dcat(pi_weights[1:H])
    x[i] ~ dbeta(alpha[z[i]], beta[z[i]])
    for (h in 1:H) {
      lcomp[i, h] <- log(pi_weights[h]) + logdensity.beta(x[i], alpha[h], beta[h])
    }
    mx[i] <- max(lcomp[i, 1:H])
    for (h in 1:H) {
      e[i, h] <- exp(lcomp[i, h] - mx[i])
    }
    log_lik[i] <- mx[i] + log(sum(e[i, 1:H]))
  }
  
  pi_weights[1:H] ~ ddirch(ones[1:H])

  for (h in 1:H) {
    alpha[h] ~ dexp(0.1)
    beta[h]  ~ dexp(0.1)
  }
}"

For a mixture model, WAIC must be computed from the marginal likelihood of each observation, integrating out the latent \(z\): \[\log p(x_i \mid \theta^{(s)}) = \log \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h^{(s)}\,\text{Beta}(x_i \mid \alpha_h^{(s)}, \beta_h^{(s)}).\]Using instead the log-density conditional on the sampled \(z_i\) (\(\log\text{Beta}(x_i\mid\alpha_{z_i},\beta_{z_i})\)) answers a different predictive question, inflates \(p_{\text{WAIC}}\), and tends to favour too many components. We compute log_lik[i] inside JAGS with the numerically stable log-sum-exp trick and monitor it. As a further advantage, the marginal density is invariant to label permutations, so this WAIC is immune to label switching.

# Reshape MCMC log-likelihood array (chains x iterations x data_points) to matrix (samples x data_points)
loglik_to_matrix <- function(loglik_samples) {
  ll <- aperm(loglik_samples, c(2, 3, 1))
  S  <- dim(ll)[1] * dim(ll)[2]
  n  <- dim(ll)[3]
  matrix(ll, nrow = S, ncol = n)
}

waic_from_loglik <- function(loglik_samples) waic(loglik_to_matrix(loglik_samples))

compute_waic_from_loglik <- function(loglik_samples)
  waic_from_loglik(loglik_samples)$estimates["waic", "Estimate"]

# Format WAIC estimates and standard errors into a summary row
ic_row <- function(w, nm) {
  e <- w$estimates
  data.frame(Model = nm,
             ELPD  = round(e["elpd_waic", "Estimate"], 1),
             p_eff = round(e["p_waic",    "Estimate"], 1),
             WAIC  = round(e["waic",      "Estimate"], 1),
             SE    = round(e["waic",      "SE"],       1))
}

# Model selection using the 1-SE rule to favor parsimony within uncertainty bounds
select_parsimonious <- function(waic_values, waic_se, complexity, n_se = 1) {
  best      <- which.min(waic_values)
  threshold <- waic_values[best] + n_se * waic_se[best]
  tied      <- which(waic_values <= threshold)
  tied[which.min(complexity[tied])]
}

# Reorder the H mixture components of every MCMC draw by ascending Beta mean
# (alpha / (alpha + beta)) to resolve label switching. Returns pi/alpha/beta as
# [H, S] matrices in which component 1 is always the lowest-mean component.
reorder_draws_by_mean <- function(samples, H) {
  pi_mat    <- matrix(samples$pi_weights, nrow = H)
  alpha_mat <- matrix(samples$alpha,      nrow = H)
  beta_mat  <- matrix(samples$beta,       nrow = H)
  for (s in seq_len(ncol(pi_mat))) {
    ord <- order(alpha_mat[, s] / (alpha_mat[, s] + beta_mat[, s]))
    pi_mat[, s]    <- pi_mat[ord, s]
    alpha_mat[, s] <- alpha_mat[ord, s]
    beta_mat[, s]  <- beta_mat[ord, s]
  }
  list(pi = pi_mat, alpha = alpha_mat, beta = beta_mat)
}

Now it is time to fit the models. All runs share the MCMC settings defined in the configuration block above (N_CHAINS, N_BURNIN, N_SAMPLES); to change any of them it is enough to edit that single block. We use the following values for the reasons below:

  • Chains (N_CHAINS = 2)
    This choice helps reduce the risk that the Markov chains become trapped near a local mode, which could lead to biased estimates. Using two JAGS chains with different initial values increases the chance of obtaining a more reliable exploration of the posterior distribution. In a final analysis, we would ideally use 3 or 4 chains.

  • Burn-in (N_BURNIN = 1000)
    This is a standard burn-in period, used to allow the chains to move away from their initial values before samples are retained for inference.

  • Iterations (N_SAMPLES = 2000)

We wrap the fitting logic in a single fit_mixture(H) helper (the \(H = 1\) case uses the single-Beta model, \(H > 1\) the mixture model) and fit the whole grid \(H = 1, \dots, 5\) with one loop, collecting the results in all_samples.

# Fit the single-Beta (H = 1) or Beta-mixture (H > 1) model for a given H
fit_mixture <- function(H) {
  if (H == 1) {
    dat       <- list(x = my_data, N = N)
    model_txt <- jags_model_H1
    vars      <- c("alpha", "beta", "log_lik")
  } else {
    dat       <- list(x = my_data, N = N, H = H, ones = rep(1, H))
    model_txt <- jags_model_mix
    vars      <- c("pi_weights", "alpha", "beta", "log_lik")
  }
  m <- jags.model(textConnection(model_txt), data = dat,
                  inits = make_inits(N_CHAINS), n.chains = N_CHAINS, quiet = TRUE)
  update(m, n.iter = N_BURNIN)
  jags.samples(m, variable.names = vars, n.iter = N_SAMPLES)
}

H_grid <- 1:5
all_samples <- lapply(H_grid, function(H) {
  cat("Fitting Model H =", H, "...\n")
  s <- fit_mixture(H)
  cat("WAIC for H =", H, ":", compute_waic_from_loglik(s$log_lik), "\n")
  s
})
## Fitting Model H = 1 ...
## WAIC for H = 1 : -1634.15 
## Fitting Model H = 2 ...
## WAIC for H = 2 : -2689.375 
## Fitting Model H = 3 ...
## WAIC for H = 3 : -3100.868 
## Fitting Model H = 4 ...
## WAIC for H = 4 : -3120.674 
## Fitting Model H = 5 ...
## WAIC for H = 5 : -3124.445
names(all_samples) <- paste0("H=", H_grid)

A single WAIC value hides its sampling uncertainty: each model has a standard error (SE), and two models whose WAIC differ by less than roughly \(1\)-\(2\) SE are statistically indistinguishable. We therefore report the full table with ELPD, the effective number of parameters p_eff (\(= p_{\text{WAIC}}\), the complexity penalty), WAIC, and its SE, and we run loo_compare, which ranks the models and gives the pairwise elpd_diff together with its se_diff. When several \(H\) values are tied within the noise, the most parsimonious among them is preferable to the bare which.min.

# Compute WAIC estimates for models with varying number of components (H)
waic_objs <- lapply(all_samples, function(s) waic_from_loglik(s$log_lik))

all_waic_values <- sapply(waic_objs, function(w) w$estimates["waic", "Estimate"])
waic_se         <- sapply(waic_objs, function(w) w$estimates["waic", "SE"])

# Generate and display the model comparison table
waic_table <- do.call(rbind, Map(ic_row, waic_objs, names(waic_objs)))
cat("Model selection: WAIC with standard errors\n")
## Model selection: WAIC with standard errors
print(waic_table, row.names = FALSE)
##  Model   ELPD p_eff    WAIC   SE
##    H=1  817.1   2.8 -1634.1 31.9
##    H=2 1344.7   3.9 -2689.4 52.0
##    H=3 1550.4   6.4 -3100.9 60.7
##    H=4 1560.3   9.5 -3120.7 60.9
##    H=5 1562.2   9.1 -3124.4 61.4
cat("\nloo_compare (differences vs the best model)\n")
## 
## loo_compare (differences vs the best model)
print(loo_compare(waic_objs))
##     elpd_diff se_diff
## H=5    0.0       0.0 
## H=4   -1.9       0.5 
## H=3  -11.8       4.0 
## H=2 -217.5      18.6 
## H=1 -745.1      32.5
# Identify the absolute minimum and the parsimonious optimal model
lowest_H <- which.min(all_waic_values)
chosen_H <- select_parsimonious(all_waic_values, waic_se, complexity = 1:5)
cat("\n Lowest-WAIC model: H =", lowest_H, "components\n")
## 
##  Lowest-WAIC model: H = 5 components
cat("Parsimonious choice (within 1 SE): H =", chosen_H, "components\n")
## Parsimonious choice (within 1 SE): H = 3 components

Now visualize the results

We plot the WAIC scores across all models alongside their \(\pm 1\) SE bounds, highlighting both the absolute minimum and the parsimonious choice.

# Define dynamic y-axis limits incorporating standard errors
ylim_waic <- range(c(all_waic_values - waic_se, all_waic_values + waic_se))

# Plot WAIC scores across model configurations
plot(1:5, all_waic_values,
     type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     ylim = ylim_waic,
     xlab = "Number of components (H)",
     ylab = "WAIC (lower is better)",
     main = "WAIC by number of components (±1 SE)",
     xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = 1:5)

# Add +/-1 SE error bars to represent estimate uncertainty
arrows(1:5, all_waic_values - waic_se, 1:5, all_waic_values + waic_se,
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05, col = "steelblue")

# Highlight absolute best configuration vs selected parsimonious model
lowest_H <- which.min(all_waic_values)
best_H   <- select_parsimonious(all_waic_values, waic_se, complexity = 1:5)
points(lowest_H, all_waic_values[lowest_H], col = "gray60", pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2)
points(best_H,   all_waic_values[best_H],   col = "tomato", pch = 19, cex = 1.8)

legend("topright",
       legend = c(paste("Lowest WAIC: H =", lowest_H),
                  paste("Chosen (1 SE): H =", best_H)),
       text.col = c("gray60", "tomato"), bty = "n")

While Information Criteria provide a quantitative measure for model selection, visual predictive checks remain crucial. The following plots compare the empirical distribution of the load factor against the implied predictive mixture density for each evaluated complexity (\(H=1\) to \(5\)). This visual comparison allows us to observe how the addition of latent components progressively captures the multimodality and the specific peaks of the empirical data, confirming the numerical results obtained via WAIC.

# Set up grid for side-by-side model comparison plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

x_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)

for (h in 1:5) {
  # Extract posterior expectations for weights and Beta parameters
  current_samples <- all_samples[[h]]
  
  if (h == 1) {
    est_pi    <- 1
    est_alpha <- mean(current_samples$alpha)
    est_beta  <- mean(current_samples$beta)
  } else {
    est_pi    <- apply(current_samples$pi_weights, 1, mean)
    est_alpha <- apply(current_samples$alpha, 1, mean)
    est_beta  <- apply(current_samples$beta, 1, mean)
  }
  
  # Draw baseline empirical distribution
  hist(my_data, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE,
       col = "lightgray", border = "white",
       xlab = "Load factor", main = paste("Mixture fit (H =", h, ")"))
  
  # Compute and overlay the implied predictive mixture density
  total_density <- rep(0, 500)
  for (c in 1:h) {
    total_density <- total_density + est_pi[c] * dbeta(x_seq, est_alpha[c], est_beta[c])
  }
  lines(x_seq, total_density, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2.5)
}

# Restore default single-plot layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Having identified the optimal and most parsimonious configuration, we now deconstruct its latent structure. The plot below illustrates the selected Beta mixture model overlaid on the empirical data. Alongside the overall mixture density (solid line), we visualize the individual, weighted Beta components (dashed lines). This explicitly shows how the different latent regimes combine to form the overall distribution of the data.

# Extract samples of the winning model
best_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]

if (best_H == 1) {
  best_pi    <- 1
  best_alpha <- mean(best_samples$alpha)
  best_beta  <- mean(best_samples$beta)
} else {
  best_pi    <- apply(best_samples$pi_weights, 1, mean)
  best_alpha <- apply(best_samples$alpha, 1, mean)
  best_beta  <- apply(best_samples$beta, 1, mean)
}

# Print the final parameters to the console
cat("\nPosterior means of the best model (H =", best_H, ")\n")
## 
## Posterior means of the best model (H = 3 )
final_params <- data.frame(Component = 1:best_H, Weight_Pi = best_pi, Alpha = best_alpha, Beta = best_beta)
print(round(final_params, 3))
##   Component Weight_Pi  Alpha   Beta
## 1         1     0.317 25.595 17.858
## 2         2     0.315 54.647 17.779
## 3         3     0.368 72.919 34.401
# Plot empirical distribution for the selected optimal model
hist(my_data, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE,
     col = "tomato", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor (hourly / daily peak)",
     main = paste("Selected Beta mixture vs. empirical density (H =", best_H, ")"))

# Calculate total mixture density and overlay constituent latent distributions
total_density <- rep(0, 500)

for (c in 1:best_H) {
  # Scale individual Beta component density by its posterior weight
  comp_density  <- best_pi[c] * dbeta(x_seq, best_alpha[c], best_beta[c])
  total_density <- total_density + comp_density
  
  # Overlay individual latent component profiles
  if (best_H > 1) {
    lines(x_seq, comp_density, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  }
}

# Draw the combined mixture density profile
lines(x_seq, total_density, col = "midnightblue", lwd = 4)

if (best_H > 1) {
  legend("topright", 
         legend = c("Empirical Data", "Overall Mixture", "Latent Components"),
         fill = c("tomato", NA, NA),
         border = c("white", NA, NA),
         col = c(NA, "midnightblue", "black"), 
         lty = c(NA, 1, 2), 
         lwd = c(NA, 4, 2),
         bty = "n")
}

Although this \(H\) was selected as the best model, the individual component curves above look implausible: they overlap heavily and do not correspond to distinct, interpretable sub-populations. This is not a failure of the fit but an artefact of how the curves were built. Each component was drawn using parameters averaged across all MCMC draws, and in a mixture the component labels are not identifiable: the sampler is free to permute them from one iteration to the next (label switching). Averaging the raw parameters therefore mixes draws coming from different permutations, blurring the components even though the overall mixture density is correct. The next section diagnoses this phenomenon and then resolves it with a post-hoc relabelling.

MCMC Diagnostics

In a mixture model the \(H\) components are exchangeable: permuting their labels leaves the joint likelihood unchanged, so the posterior has up to \(H!\) equivalent modes, one for each relabelling of the same solution. When two MCMC chains independently explore different permutations, the raw parameter traces cross and swap between iterations, a phenomenon known as label switching. Naively averaging parameters across such chains would blend draws from different permutations, producing meaningless component summaries.

Although the overall mixture density accurately captures the empirical data, directly averaging the raw component parameters across all MCMC iterations can therefore be misleading. To diagnose whether label switching is occurring, we inspect the trace plots.

raw_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]

raw_pi_mat    <- matrix(raw_samples$pi_weights, nrow = best_H)
raw_alpha_mat <- matrix(raw_samples$alpha, nrow = best_H)
raw_beta_mat  <- matrix(raw_samples$beta, nrow = best_H)

alpha_array <- raw_samples$alpha
beta_array  <- raw_samples$beta
pi_array <- raw_samples$pi_weights

n_iter   <- dim(alpha_array)[2]
n_chains <- dim(alpha_array)[3]

chain_colors <- 1:n_chains

# Diagnostics for alpha.
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (h in 1:best_H) {

Now we calculate Gelman-Rubin coefficient, \(\hat{R}\) :

calculate_rhat_table <- function(alpha_array, beta_array, pi_array, best_H, n_chains) {
  
  # Vectors to store the point estimates
  rhat_alpha <- numeric(best_H)
  rhat_beta  <- numeric(best_H)
  rhat_pi    <- numeric(best_H)
  
  for (h in 1:best_H) {
    # Gelman-Rubin Diagnostic for Alpha
    chain_list_alpha <- list()
    for (c in 1:n_chains) {
      chain_list_alpha[[c]] <- mcmc(alpha_array[h, , c])
    }
    gr_alpha <- gelman.diag(as.mcmc.list(chain_list_alpha), autoburnin = FALSE)
    rhat_alpha[h] <- gr_alpha$psrf[1, 1] # Extract Point Estimate
    
    # For Beta
    chain_list_beta <- list()
    for (c in 1:n_chains) {
      chain_list_beta[[c]] <- mcmc(beta_array[h, , c])
    }
    gr_beta <- gelman.diag(as.mcmc.list(chain_list_beta), autoburnin = FALSE)
    rhat_beta[h] <- gr_beta$psrf[1, 1] # Extract Point Estimate
    
    # For Pi
    chain_list_pi <- list()
    for (c in 1:n_chains) {
      chain_list_pi[[c]] <- mcmc(pi_array[h, , c])
    }
    gr_pi <- gelman.diag(as.mcmc.list(chain_list_pi), autoburnin = FALSE)
    rhat_pi[h] <- gr_pi$psrf[1, 1] # Extract Point Estimate
  }
  
  # Generate variable names dynamically
  alpha_names <- paste0("alpha[", 1:best_H, "]")
  beta_names  <- paste0("beta[", 1:best_H, "]")
  pi_names    <- paste0("pi[", 1:best_H, "]")
  
  # Assemble diagnostics into a single dataframe for presentation
  rhat_table <- data.frame(
    Variable = c(alpha_names, beta_names, pi_names),
    Raw_R_hat = round(c(rhat_alpha, rhat_beta, rhat_pi), 4)
  )
  
  return(rhat_table)
}

# Evaluate convergence using the 3D raw sample arrays from JAGS
rhat_table_output <- calculate_rhat_table(raw_samples$alpha, 
                                          raw_samples$beta, 
                                          raw_samples$pi_weights, 
                                          best_H, 
                                          n_chains)

print(rhat_table_output, row.names = FALSE)
##  Variable Raw_R_hat
##  alpha[1]   17.2157
##  alpha[2]   19.6549
##  alpha[3]    8.2966
##   beta[1]   18.8681
##   beta[2]   20.7348
##   beta[3]    1.1668
##     pi[1]    5.9261
##     pi[2]    5.7758
##     pi[3]    1.0233

The traces show the characteristic label-switching signature: chains running on separate tracks that occasionally cross, and multimodal marginal densities for each raw component parameter. The \(\hat{R}\) values in the table above, several of which exceed the conventional 1.10 threshold, formally confirm this instability.

At this point two explanations are possible:

  • the chains genuinely failed to mix and explore the posterior

  • the high \(\hat{R}\) is a statistical artifact caused by the chains sampling from different, but equivalent, label permutations of a well-mixed sampler.

To distinguish between the two explanations, we evaluate \(\hat{R}\) and the Effective Sample Size (ESS) on the marginal log-likelihood \(\ell^{(s)} = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_i \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(s)})\). This scalar is a function of the full mixture density, which is invariant to any relabelling of the components, so it is unaffected by label switching.

loglik_array <- raw_samples$log_lik

n_iter   <- dim(loglik_array)[2]
n_chains <- dim(loglik_array)[3]

# Marginalize out component labels by summing point-wise log-likelihoods
global_loglik <- apply(loglik_array, c(2, 3), sum)

# Format global log-likelihood iterations into an mcmc.list object
loglik_chains <- list()
for (c in 1:n_chains) {
  loglik_chains[[c]] <- mcmc(global_loglik[, c])
}
loglik_mcmc_list <- as.mcmc.list(loglik_chains)

# Compute permutation-invariant convergence statistics
rhat_loglik <- gelman.diag(loglik_mcmc_list, autoburnin = FALSE)$psrf[1, 1]
ess_loglik  <- effectiveSize(loglik_mcmc_list)

# Assemble diagnostics table
likelihood_diagnostic_table <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("R-hat ", "ESS  "),
  Value  = c(round(rhat_loglik, 4), round(ess_loglik, 2))
)

cat("Likelihood Convergence Diagnostic (Permutation-Invariant Scale)\n\n")
## Likelihood Convergence Diagnostic (Permutation-Invariant Scale)
print(likelihood_diagnostic_table, row.names = FALSE)
##  Metric    Value
##  R-hat    1.0446
##   ESS   518.6700

The table above shows \(\hat{R} \approx 1\) and a healthy ESS, confirming that the sampler has reached global convergence. The instability in the raw component parameters is therefore purely an artifact of the chains sampling from different label permutations of the same posterior mode.

Post-hoc re-labelling

To restore parameter identifiability for reporting, we apply a post-hoc re-labelling: at each MCMC draw we sort the \(H\) components by their theoretical Beta mean,

\[\mathbb{E}[X_h] = \frac{\alpha_h}{\alpha_h + \beta_h},\]

from smallest to largest. This criterion is the natural choice because \(\mathbb{E}[X_h]\) is the “location” of component \(h\) on the \((0,1)\) interval: it identifies whether a component captures low, medium, or high load-factor observations regardless of which numeric label JAGS happened to assign at that step. After re-ordering, “Component 1” consistently refers to the lowest-mean Beta across all draws and chains, making per-component summaries comparable. This post-hoc step does not alter the fit: the mixture density and the WAIC are unchanged; it only resolves the label ambiguity for interpretation.

best_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]

# Reorder every draw by ascending Beta mean so component labels are consistent
ord      <- reorder_draws_by_mean(best_samples, best_H)
S_tot <- ncol(ord$pi)
x_seq    <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)

component_curves <- array(0, dim = c(best_H, S_tot, length(x_seq)))

cat("Sorting MCMC chains and calculating posterior densities...\n")
## Sorting MCMC chains and calculating posterior densities...
for (s in 1:S_tot) {
  for (h in 1:best_H) {
    component_curves[h, s, ] <- ord$pi[h, s] *
      dbeta(x_seq, ord$alpha[h, s], ord$beta[h, s])
  }
}

# Average curves over iterations to obtain point estimates of latent profiles
final_components      <- apply(component_curves, c(1, 3), mean)
final_overall_mixture <- colSums(final_components)

# PLOTTING

hist(my_data, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE,
     col = "tomato", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor (hourly / daily peak)",
     main = paste("Mixture components after post-hoc relabelling (H =", best_H, ")"))

# Overlay identified, sorted latent components
for (h in 1:best_H) {
  lines(x_seq, final_components[h, ], col = COMPONENT_COLS[h], lty = 2, lwd = 2.5)
}

# Overlay final posterior predictive mixture profile
lines(x_seq, final_overall_mixture, col = "midnightblue", lwd = 4)

legend_labels <- c("Empirical data", "Overall mixture", paste("Component", 1:best_H))
legend_colors <- c(NA, "midnightblue", COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H])
legend_lines  <- c(NA, 1, rep(2, best_H))
legend_widths <- c(NA, 4, rep(2.5, best_H))

legend("topright", 
       legend = legend_labels,

Having resolved the label-switching ambiguity, we can now safely extract meaningful posterior summaries for each individual component. The final step is to isolate these latent Beta distributions to examine their specific profiles and parameter uncertainties.

Below, we visualize each sorted component independently, alongside its expected weight, shape parameters (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)), and theoretical mean. Furthermore, we compute the 95% equal-tailed credible intervals for the parameters, providing a rigorous quantification of the posterior uncertainty for each identified cluster within the data.

best_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]

# Reorder MCMC draws post-hoc by ascending component means to resolve label switching
ord       <- reorder_draws_by_mean(best_samples, best_H)
pi_ord    <- ord$pi
alpha_ord <- ord$alpha
beta_ord  <- ord$beta

# Helper to compute posterior expectations and 95% equal-tailed credible intervals
summ <- function(m) cbind(mean = rowMeans(m),
                          lwr  = apply(m, 1, quantile, 0.025),
                          upr  = apply(m, 1, quantile, 0.975))
A <- summ(alpha_ord); B <- summ(beta_ord); P <- summ(pi_ord)
comp_mean <- A[, "mean"] / (A[, "mean"] + B[, "mean"])

# Generate summary table for the identified mixture components
tab <- data.frame(
  Component = 1:best_H,
  Weight    = round(P[, "mean"], 3),
  Alpha     = round(A[, "mean"], 3),
  Beta      = round(B[, "mean"], 3),
  Mean      = round(comp_mean, 3),
  Alpha_CI  = paste0("[", round(A[, "lwr"], 2), ", ", round(A[, "upr"], 2), "]"),
  Beta_CI   = paste0("[", round(B[, "lwr"], 2), ", ", round(B[, "upr"], 2), "]")
)
cat("Component parameters (posterior mean, 95% credible interval)\n")
## Component parameters (posterior mean, 95% credible interval)
print(tab, row.names = FALSE)

x_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)

# Evaluate densities using posterior parameter expectations
dens_mat <- sapply(1:best_H, function(h) dbeta(x_seq, A[h, "mean"], B[h, "mean"]))

ylim_common <- c(0, 10)
xlim_common <- c(0, 1)

par(mfrow = c(ceiling(best_H / 2), 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

Prior Sensitivity Analysis

The mixture model results depend on two hyperparameter choices: the rate \(\lambda\) of the Exponential prior on the shape parameters (\(\alpha_h, \beta_h\)), and the concentration \(c\) of the symmetric Dirichlet prior on the mixture weights \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\). A sensitivity analysis checks whether these choices are driving the conclusions — specifically, whether the selected \(H\), the inferred component shapes, and the WAIC change when the priors become more or less diffuse. If results are stable across settings the inference is data-driven; if they shift, the prior is influential and the choice requires more careful justification.

We refit the best-\(H\) model under four configurations, varying one hyperparameter at a time while holding the rest fixed:

Setting \(\lambda\) Dir. conc. \(c\) Interpretation
Reference 0.10 1.0 Current prior: \(\mathbb{E}[\alpha_h] = 10\)
Very diffuse 0.01 1.0 Shape parameters up to \(\sim\!200\) allowed
Informative 1.00 1.0 Shape parameters concentrated near 1
Sparse Dirichlet 0.10 0.1 Encourages one dominant component 
# Parameterised JAGS model
jags_model_sens <- "
model {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    z[i] ~ dcat(pi_weights[1:H])
    x[i] ~ dbeta(alpha[z[i]], beta[z[i]])
    for (h in 1:H) {
      lcomp[i, h] <- log(pi_weights[h]) + logdensity.beta(x[i], alpha[h], beta[h])
    }
    mx[i]      <- max(lcomp[i, 1:H])
    for (h in 1:H) { e[i, h] <- exp(lcomp[i, h] - mx[i]) }
    log_lik[i] <- mx[i] + log(sum(e[i, 1:H]))
  }
  pi_weights[1:H] ~ ddirch(dir_conc[1:H])
  for (h in 1:H) {
    alpha[h] ~ dexp(lambda_exp)
    beta[h]  ~ dexp(lambda_exp)
  }
}
"

# Helper: fit best_H model with given hyperparameters
fit_sensitivity <- function(H, lambda_exp, dir_conc_val) {
  dat <- list(x          = my_data,
              N          = N,
              H          = H,
              lambda_exp = lambda_exp,
              dir_conc   = rep(dir_conc_val, H))
  m <- jags.model(textConnection(jags_model_sens), data = dat,
                  inits = make_inits(N_CHAINS), n.chains = N_CHAINS, quiet = TRUE)
  update(m, n.iter = N_BURNIN)
  jags.samples(m, variable.names = c("pi_weights", "alpha", "beta", "log_lik"),
               n.iter = N_SAMPLES)
}

# Helper: label-switching-invariant posterior predictive density
compute_ppd_sens <- function(samps, H, x_grid) {
  pi_m <- matrix(samps$pi_weights, nrow = H)
  al_m <- matrix(samps$alpha,      nrow = H)
  be_m <- matrix(samps$beta,       nrow = H)
  S    <- ncol(pi_m)
  rowMeans(sapply(seq_len(S), function(s) {
    d <- numeric(length(x_grid))
    for (h in seq_len(H))
      d <- d + pi_m[h, s] * dbeta(x_grid, al_m[h, s], be_m[h, s])
    d
  }))
}
sens_settings <- list(
  list(label = "Reference (λ=0.1, c=1.0)",     lambda = 0.10, dir = 1.0),
  list(label = "Very diffuse (λ=0.01, c=1.0)", lambda = 0.01, dir = 1.0),
  list(label = "Informative (λ=1.0, c=1.0)",   lambda = 1.00, dir = 1.0),
  list(label = "Sparse Dir. (λ=0.1, c=0.1)",   lambda = 0.10, dir = 0.1)
)

# Setting 1 is already fitted as best_H in Task 1 — reuse it directly.
# Settings 2-4 are refitted with the parameterised model above.
sens_samples <- vector("list", length(sens_settings))
sens_samples[[1]] <- all_samples[[best_H]]

for (j in 2:length(sens_settings)) {
  s <- sens_settings[[j]]
  cat("Sensitivity fit:", s$label, "\n")
  sens_samples[[j]] <- fit_sensitivity(best_H, s$lambda, s$dir)
}

Task 2

Objective: overlay the posterior predictive density on the empirical histogram and verify that the modes (the peaks of the data) are recovered by the model selected in Task 1.

Posterior predictive density

The fully Bayesian overlay is the posterior predictive density, obtained by averaging the mixture density over the entire posterior (the latent \(z\) is already integrated out inside each mixture term): \[p(\tilde x \mid \text{data}) = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \sum_{h=1}^H \pi_h^{(s)}\,\text{Beta}\!\left(\tilde x \mid \alpha_h^{(s)}, \beta_h^{(s)}\right).\]

We average the densities, not the parameters. This way the curve accounts for posterior uncertainty.

best_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]
x_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 600)

if (best_H == 1) {
  alpha_s <- as.vector(best_samples$alpha)
  beta_s  <- as.vector(best_samples$beta)
  S_tot   <- length(alpha_s)
  ppd     <- rowMeans(sapply(seq_len(S_tot),
                             function(s) dbeta(x_grid, alpha_s[s], beta_s[s])))
} else {
  pi_mat    <- matrix(best_samples$pi_weights, nrow = best_H)
  alpha_mat <- matrix(best_samples$alpha,      nrow = best_H)
  beta_mat  <- matrix(best_samples$beta,       nrow = best_H)
  S_tot     <- ncol(pi_mat)

  # full mixture density for a single draw s
  mix_density <- function(s) {
    d <- numeric(length(x_grid))
    for (h in 1:best_H)
      d <- d + pi_mat[h, s] * dbeta(x_grid, alpha_mat[h, s], beta_mat[h, s])
    d
  }
  # posterior predictive = average over all draws
  ppd <- rowMeans(sapply(seq_len(S_tot), mix_density))
}

Overlay and mode recovery

# A point is a local maximum if it exceeds both its neighbours
local_maxima <- function(xx, yy) {
  n   <- length(yy)
  hit <- which(yy[2:(n - 1)] > yy[1:(n - 2)] & yy[2:(n - 1)] > yy[3:n]) + 1
  xx[hit]
}

ppd_modes <- local_maxima(x_grid, ppd)
cat("Posterior-predictive modes: ", round(ppd_modes, 3), "\n")
## Posterior-predictive modes:  0.567 0.751
hist(my_data, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE,
     col = "lightgray", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor (hourly / daily peak)",
     main = paste("Posterior predictive overlay (H =", best_H, ")"))
lines(x_grid, ppd, col = "midnightblue", lwd = 3)

abline(v = ppd_modes, col = "tomato", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
points(ppd_modes, approx(x_grid, ppd, ppd_modes)$y, pch = 19, col = "tomato")

legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.9,
       legend = c("Posterior predictive", "Predictive modes"),
       col = c("midnightblue", "tomato"),
       lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(3, 1.5), pch = c(NA, 19))

The posterior predictive curve (blue) is the Bayesian predictive density for a new observation given the data. The red dashed lines mark its local maxima: since they align with the visible peaks of the histogram the model has successfully recovered the modes of the data.

Task 3

Objective (post-hoc exploration): assign each observation to its maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) component, then plot the empirical fraction of observations in each component as a function of hour.

In a mixture the latent indicator \(z_i\) is the cluster label, so this step means assigning every observation to its most likely component and studying how those assignments vary across hours of the day.

Avoiding label switching. We do not use the raw \(z_i\) from a single MCMC draw (labels permute across iterations). Instead we compute posterior responsibilities using the components re-ordered by their mean at every draw (the same ordering used in the plots above): \[r_{ih} = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \frac{\pi^{(s)}_{(h)}\,\text{Beta}(x_i\mid\alpha^{(s)}_{(h)},\beta^{(s)}_{(h)})}{\sum_k \pi^{(s)}_{(k)}\,\text{Beta}(x_i\mid\alpha^{(s)}_{(k)},\beta^{(s)}_{(k)})}, \qquad \hat z_i = \arg\max_h r_{ih},\] where \((h)\) denotes the \(h\)-th component from the left (smallest mean). This makes “Component 1” consistently the lowest-mean component and the MAP assignment stable across chains.

best_samples <- all_samples[[best_H]]

# Components sorted by increasing mean at every draw (component 1 = lowest mean)
ord   <- reorder_draws_by_mean(best_samples, best_H)
S_tot <- ncol(ord$pi)

# mean responsibilities: resp[i, h] = P(component h | x_i)
resp <- matrix(0, nrow = N, ncol = best_H)

for (s in 1:S_tot) {
  w <- matrix(0, nrow = N, ncol = best_H)
  for (h in 1:best_H) {
    w[, h] <- ord$pi[h, s] * dbeta(my_data, ord$alpha[h, s], ord$beta[h, s])
  }
  w <- w / rowSums(w)   # normalise -> responsibilities at this draw
  resp <- resp + w
}
resp <- resp / S_tot

# MAP assignment: each observation to its most probable component
z_map <- apply(resp, 1, which.max)

cat("Cluster sizes (MAP assignment):\n")
## Cluster sizes (MAP assignment):
print(table(factor(z_map, levels = 1:best_H)))
## 
##   1   2   3 
## 755 784 461

Empirical fraction of observations in each component as a function of the hour of the day.

hours <- lf_fit$hour

# hour x component contingency table, then row-proportions (each hour sums to 1)
tab      <- table(factor(hours, levels = 0:23), factor(z_map, levels = 1:best_H))
frac_mat <- prop.table(tab, margin = 1)

matplot(0:23, as.matrix(frac_mat), type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1,
        col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], lwd = 2,
        xlab = "Hour of day",
        ylab = "Fraction of observations",
        main = "Component fractions by hour (MAP assignment)")
legend("topleft", legend = paste("Component", 1:best_H),
       col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n")

A complementary view: raw observations coloured by their MAP component, plotted against hour.

plot(jitter(hours, amount = 0.3), my_data,
     col  = adjustcolor(COMPONENT_COLS[z_map], alpha.f = 0.45),
     pch  = 19, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Hour of day", ylab = "Load factor",
     main = "Load factor by hour, coloured by MAP component",
     xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 23, by = 2))
legend("topleft", legend = paste("Component", 1:best_H),
       col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)

Task 4

Objective (advanced): fit a second model that performs classification on hour, using the component assignment from Task 3 as the response variable, and plot the predicted probability of each component as a function of hour. We then compare these predicted curves with the empirical fractions of Task 3 and discuss the result.

From clustering to a supervised model on hour

In Task 3 the latent label \(\hat z_i \in \{1, \dots, H\}\) was obtained unsupervised, from the load factor alone. Here we turn the question around and ask: how predictable is the component label from the time of day? We treat \(\hat z_i\) as the response of a supervised model whose only covariate is hour.

Because the response has \(H > 2\) levels, this is a multinomial (multi-class) logistic regression, the natural generalisation of the binomial logit to more than two categories. We keep one component as the reference category (here \(h = 1\), the lowest-mean component) and model the log-odds of every other component against it.

hour is a cyclic variable: hour \(23\) is adjacent to hour \(0\). Encoding it as a raw integer would wrongly treat midnight and 11pm as far apart, so we expand it on a Fourier basis of period \(24\), \[s_{ik} = \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi k\,\mathrm{hour}_i}{24}\right), \qquad c_{ik} = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k\,\mathrm{hour}_i}{24}\right), \qquad k = 1, \dots, K,\] and use these \(2K\) functions as covariates. A small number of harmonics \(K\) is enough; we pick \(K\) by WAIC, exactly as we chose \(H\) in Task 1.

Mathematical formulation

For observation \(i\) and component \(h\) the linear predictor is \[\eta_{i,h} = \beta_{0,h} + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\alpha_{k,h}\,s_{ik} + \gamma_{k,h}\,c_{ik}\bigr),\] with the reference class constrained to zero, \(\beta_{0,1} = 0\) and \(\alpha_{k,1} = \gamma_{k,1} = 0\) for all \(k\). The class probabilities are recovered with the softmax transform \[P(z_i = h) = \frac{\exp(\eta_{i,h})}{\sum_{j=1}^{H}\exp(\eta_{i,j})},\] which automatically adds up to 1. By construction the predicted probabilities are periodic in hour with period \(24\), exactly like the empirical curves of Task 3.

We place vague \(\mathcal{N}(0, 0.01)\) priors (in JAGS precision parametrisation, i.e. variance \(100\)) on the \(H - 1\) free coefficient blocks, the same weakly informative choice used for the regression and mixture models in the lab.

On label switching. The response \(\hat z_i\) comes from the components already re-ordered by increasing mean in Task 3, so “component 1” is consistently the lowest-mean cluster. The labels are therefore stable and the comparison between predicted curves and empirical fractions is well defined.

Design matrices and JAGS model

We pre-compute the sine/cosine matrices \(S\) and \(C\) in R and pass them to JAGS as data; the response is z_map from Task 3 and the covariate is hours (aligned with my_data). The JAGS code is the categorical-logit skeleton: z[i] ~ dcat(pp[i, 1:H]) with pp[i, ] built from the softmax of the Fourier linear predictors. We also monitor the marginal per-observation log-likelihood log_lik[i] = log(pp[i, z[i]]) so the same WAIC machinery from Task 1 can select \(K\).

jags_model_logit <- "
model {
  for (i in 1:n) {
    z[i] ~ dcat(pp[i, 1:H])
    for (h in 1:H) {
      eta[i, h]    <- beta0[h] +
                      inprod(alpha[1:K, h], S[i, 1:K]) +
                      inprod(gamma[1:K, h], C[i, 1:K])
      expEta[i, h] <- exp(eta[i, h])
      pp[i, h]     <- expEta[i, h] / sum(expEta[i, 1:H])
    }
   log_lik[i] <- log(pp[i, z[i]])
  }

  beta0[1] <- 0
  for (k in 1:K) { alpha[k, 1] <- 0; gamma[k, 1] <- 0 }

  for (h in 2:H) {
    beta0[h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    for (k in 1:K) {
      alpha[k, h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
      gamma[k, h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    }
  }
}
"

Helper that builds the Fourier design for a given number of harmonics \(K\), fits the model and returns the monitored samples.

# Reshape the monitored logit coefficients of one fit into per-draw arrays:
# beta0 as [H, S], alpha and gamma as [K, H, S].
reshape_logit_coefs <- function(fit, H, K) {
  beta0_s <- matrix(fit$beta0, nrow = H)
  S       <- ncol(beta0_s)
  list(beta0 = beta0_s,
       alpha = array(fit$alpha, dim = c(K, H, S)),
       gamma = array(fit$gamma, dim = c(K, H, S)))
}

# Posterior-mean class probabilities P(component | hour) for a Fourier design,
# averaging the softmax over all posterior draws (not the coefficients).
predict_logit_probs <- function(coefs, design, H) {
  n <- nrow(design$S)
  S <- ncol(coefs$beta0)
  P <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = H)
  for (s in seq_len(S)) {
    eta <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = H)
    for (h in seq_len(H))
      eta[, h] <- coefs$beta0[h, s] +
                  design$S %*% coefs$alpha[, h, s] +
                  design$C %*% coefs$gamma[, h, s]
    ex <- exp(eta)
    P  <- P + ex / rowSums(ex)
  }
  P / S
}

fit_logit_K <- function(K) {
  fb  <- fourier_design(hours, K)   # [N, K] design; stays 2-D even when K = 1
  dat <- list(z = z_map, n = N, H = best_H, K = K, S = fb$S, C = fb$C)
  m <- jags.model(textConnection(jags_model_logit), data = dat,
                  inits = make_inits(N_CHAINS), n.chains = N_CHAINS, quiet = TRUE)
  update(m, n.iter = N_BURNIN)
  jags.samples(m, variable.names = c("beta0", "alpha", "gamma", "log_lik"),
               n.iter = N_SAMPLES)
}

Model selection over the number of harmonics

We fit \(K \in \{1, \dots, 5\}\) and compare them with WAIC, with the same machinery used in Task 1. A wider grid lets us see the elbow rather than assume it: a larger \(K\) buys a wigglier probability profile, and we expect WAIC to stop improving once the harmonics start fitting noise. As in Task 1 we report WAIC with its SE and p_eff, and loo_compare with elpd_diff/se_diff, then pick the simplest \(K\) that is not clearly beaten.

K_grid     <- 1:5
logit_fits <- vector("list", length(K_grid))
waic_klist <- vector("list", length(K_grid))

for (j in seq_along(K_grid)) {
  K <- K_grid[j]
  cat("Fitting multinomial logit with K =", K, "harmonic(s)...\n")
  logit_fits[[j]] <- fit_logit_K(K)
  waic_klist[[j]] <- waic_from_loglik(logit_fits[[j]]$log_lik)
}

names(waic_klist) <- paste0("K=", K_grid)

# Precise vectors + comparison table (ELPD, p_eff, WAIC, SE)
waic_logit  <- sapply(waic_klist, function(w) w$estimates["waic", "Estimate"])
waic_logit_se <- sapply(waic_klist, function(w) w$estimates["waic", "SE"])
logit_table <- do.call(rbind, Map(ic_row, waic_klist, names(waic_klist)))

cat("\nModel selection: WAIC with standard errors\n")
##

print(logit_table, row.names = FALSE)
##  Model   ELPD p_eff   WAIC   SE
##    K=1 -678.0   9.5 1356.1 80.7

print(loo_compare(waic_klist))

lowest_K <- K_grid[which.min(waic_logit)]
best_K   <- K_grid[select_parsimonious(waic_logit, waic_logit_se, complexity = K_grid)]

To visualize this selection, we plot the WAIC-vs-\(K\) curve with \(\pm 1\) SE bounds, reading the optimal elbow directly from the diagnostic graph:

ylim_k <- range(c(waic_logit - waic_logit_se, waic_logit + waic_logit_se))
plot(K_grid, waic_logit, type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 1.4,
     col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, ylim = ylim_k,
     xlab = "Number of harmonics (K)", ylab = "WAIC (lower is better)",
     main = "WAIC by number of harmonics (±1 SE)",
     xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = K_grid)
arrows(K_grid, waic_logit - waic_logit_se, K_grid, waic_logit + waic_logit_se,
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05, col = "steelblue")
points(lowest_K, waic_logit[which.min(waic_logit)],
       col = "gray60", pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2)
points(best_K, waic_logit[which(K_grid == best_K)],
       col = "tomato", pch = 19, cex = 1.8)
legend("topright",
       legend = c(paste("Lowest WAIC: K =", lowest_K),
                  paste("Chosen (1 SE): K =", best_K)),
       text.col = c("gray60", "tomato"), bty = "n")

Predicted probability curves

To construct the predictive curves, we evaluate the posterior mean of \(P(z = h)\) across a continuous grid of hour values spanning from 0 to 23. Crucially, for each posterior draw, we reconstruct the Fourier components, form the linear predictors from the sampled coefficients, apply the softmax transformation, and then average the resulting probabilities. Averaging the probabilities rather than the raw coefficients ensures that the final curves correctly propagate the non-linear posterior uncertainty.

best_fit  <- logit_fits[[which(K_grid == best_K)]]
best_coef <- reshape_logit_coefs(best_fit, best_H, best_K)

# Posterior-mean predicted probabilities P(z = h | hour) on the hour grid
hour_grid <- 0:23
P_pred    <- predict_logit_probs(best_coef, fourier_design(hour_grid, best_K), best_H)

matplot(hour_grid, P_pred, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2.5,
        col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "Hour of day", ylab = "Predicted P(component | hour)",
        main = paste0("Multinomial logit fit (K = ", best_K, ")"))
legend("topright", legend = paste("Component", 1:best_H),
       col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], lwd = 2.5, lty = 1, bty = "n")

Comparison with the empirical fractions of Task 3

Finally, we overlay the smooth logit-predicted curves (solid lines) onto the raw empirical fractions derived from Task 3 (points). If the two plot spaces agree, it indicates that the component assignment is effectively a deterministic function of the hour, meaning the supervised logit model has successfully learned a clean, periodic representation of the noisy empirical proportions.

matplot(0:23, as.matrix(frac_mat), type = "p", pch = 19,
        col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "Hour of day", ylab = "Fraction / predicted probability",
        main = "Predicted probabilities vs. empirical fractions")
matlines(hour_grid, P_pred, lty = 1, lwd = 2.5, col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H])
legend("topright",
       legend = c(paste("Component", 1:best_H), "Empirical (Task 3)", "Logit (Task 4)"),
       col = c(COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], "gray40", "gray40"),
       pch = c(rep(19, best_H), 19, NA),
       lty = c(rep(NA, best_H), NA, 1),
       lwd = c(rep(NA, best_H), NA, 2.5),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

The solid logit curves closely track the empirical points, illustrating clear temporal dynamics: the low-mean component dominates during the night and steadily decreases as the day progresses, whereas the high-mean component rises to dominate around the daily peak hours (with intermediate components bridging the transition).

This strong alignment is theoretically expected, as both approaches estimate the identical quantity, \(P(\text{component}\mid\text{hour})\). However, the differences in how they estimate it are highly informative. Task 3 calculates this by discretely counting observations hour-by-hour, yielding a noisy profile. Conversely, Task 4 fits a smooth, strictly periodic model that borrows statistical strength across adjacent hours via the Fourier basis.

The minor discrepancies that occur between the curves, are typically found at these low-sample hours where the empirical estimate is least robust.

Prediction Exercise

The multinomial logistic regression in Task 4 was fitted on the same observations used to derive the response \(\hat z_i\), so the WAIC is an in-sample criterion. A held-out prediction exercise provides an out-of-sample check: it quantifies how well the model generalises to unseen hour-component pairs and whether hour carries genuinely predictive information beyond the unconditional class frequencies.

Experimental Setup: We randomly split the \(N\) observations into a training set (80%) and a test set (20%), keeping the hour and z_map pairs aligned. The multinomial logit with \(K = K_\text{best}\) harmonics is refitted on the training subset only. The resulting posterior is then used to predict the component label of each test observation from its hour.

Evaluation Metrics: We report the log-loss on the test set, \[\text{log-loss} = -\frac{1}{N_\text{test}}\sum_{i \in \text{test}} \log \hat{P}(z_i = \hat z_{\text{map},i} \mid \text{hour}_i),\]

and the accuracy (fraction of correctly predicted MAP labels). Both are compared against a null baseline that ignores hour entirely and always predicts the empirical class proportions observed in the training set.

set.seed(42)
n_train_pred <- floor(0.8 * N)
train_pred   <- sample(seq_len(N), n_train_pred)
test_pred    <- setdiff(seq_len(N), train_pred)
n_test_pred  <- length(test_pred)

# Fourier designs for the training and test subsets
fb_tr <- fourier_design(hours[train_pred], best_K)
fb_te <- fourier_design(hours[test_pred],  best_K)

# Refit the logit on the training subset only
dat_tr <- list(z = z_map[train_pred], n = n_train_pred,
               H = best_H, K = best_K, S = fb_tr$S, C = fb_tr$C)
m_tr   <- jags.model(textConnection(jags_model_logit), data = dat_tr,
                     inits = make_inits(N_CHAINS), n.chains = N_CHAINS, quiet = TRUE)
update(m_tr, n.iter = N_BURNIN)
samp_tr <- jags.samples(m_tr,
                        variable.names = c("beta0", "alpha", "gamma"),
                        n.iter = N_SAMPLES)
# Reshape the training-fit coefficients and predict on the test set [n_test x H]
coef_tr <- reshape_logit_coefs(samp_tr, best_H, best_K)
P_te    <- predict_logit_probs(coef_tr, fb_te, best_H)

# Log-loss and accuracy
z_te        <- z_map[test_pred]
pred_probs  <- sapply(seq_len(n_test_pred), function(i) P_te[i, z_te[i]])
log_loss_te <- -mean(log(pmax(pred_probs, 1e-10)))

z_pred_te   <- apply(P_te, 1, which.max)
acc_te      <- mean(z_pred_te == z_te)

# Null baseline: empirical class proportions from training set
train_props  <- tabulate(z_map[train_pred], nbins = best_H) / n_train_pred
baseline_ll  <- -mean(log(pmax(train_props[z_te], 1e-10)))
baseline_acc <- max(tabulate(z_map[train_pred])) / n_train_pred

pred_table <- data.frame(
  Metric   = c("Log-loss (lower is better)", "Accuracy (higher is better)"),
  Model    = round(c(log_loss_te, acc_te),       3),
  Baseline = round(c(baseline_ll, baseline_acc), 3)
)
cat("Prediction exercise (test set, n =", n_test_pred, ")\n")
## Prediction exercise (test set, n = 400 )
print(pred_table, row.names = FALSE)
##                       Metric Model Baseline
##   Log-loss (lower is better) 0.276    1.114
##  Accuracy (higher is better) 0.900    0.395

The metrics indicate that hour is a genuinely informative covariate.
This final plot compares the probability curves estimated exclusively from the 80% training subset against the empirical fractions derived from the full dataset (Task 3), showing strong agreement between the two.

# Compare probability curves from the train-only fit against the
# empirical fractions derived from the full data in Task 3.
# Close agreement means the model generalises: the periodic pattern
# learned on 80% of the data reproduces the full-data proportions.
hour_grid_p <- 0:23
P_grid <- predict_logit_probs(coef_tr, fourier_design(hour_grid_p, best_K), best_H)

matplot(0:23, as.matrix(frac_mat), type = "p", pch = 19,
        col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "Hour of day",
        ylab = "Fraction / predicted probability",
        main = "Train-fitted logit vs. empirical fractions")
matlines(hour_grid_p, P_grid, lty = 1, lwd = 2.5, col = COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H])
legend("topright",
       legend = c(paste("Component", 1:best_H),
                  "Empirical fractions", "Logit"),
       col = c(COMPONENT_COLS[1:best_H], "gray40", "gray40"),
       pch = c(rep(19, best_H), 19, NA),
       lty = c(rep(NA,  best_H), NA,  1),
       lwd = c(rep(NA,  best_H), NA,  2.5),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
